title: Intersection with an ideal generated by a regular sequence modulo another ideal
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $I$ an ideal of $R$, and $g_1,\dots,g_m\in R$ elements whose images in $R/I$ form a regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. Put $K=(g_1,\dots,g_m)\subseteq R$. Then $I\cap K=IK$ as ideals of $R$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 0665 (lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient), lines 7471-7494, specialized using Tag 062F (lemma-regular-koszul-regular), lines 7265-7298, and Tag 0CEM (lemma-koszul-regular-H1-regular), lines 7300-7308. Source read from /tmp/stacks-project/more-algebra.tex on 2026-10-10.

proof.text: *The images are $H_1$-regular in $A/I$.* Write $A$ for the ring $R$ of the statement (the source's notation), $\bar A=A/I$, and $\bar x$ for the image of $x\in A$ in $\bar A$; the Koszul complexes below are written $K_\bullet(-)$, not to be confused with the ideal $K=(g_1,\dots,g_m)$. By hypothesis $\bar g_1,\dots,\bar g_m$ is a regular sequence in $\bar A$ [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]: for each $i$, multiplication by $\bar g_i$ is injective on $\bar A/(\bar g_1,\dots,\bar g_{i-1})$. So [lem-weil-pbc-regular-sequence-koszul-regular] (Stacks 062F, with ring $\bar A$ and $M=\bar A$) shows that $\bar g_1,\dots,\bar g_m$ is Koszul-regular, i.e. $H_i(K_\bullet(\bar A,\bar g_1,\dots,\bar g_m))=0$ for all $i\neq0$ [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence]. Taking $i=1$, it is $H_1$-regular (Stacks 0CEM: 'immediate from the definition'): $H_1(K_\bullet(\bar A,\bar g_\bullet))=0$.

source.place: Lemma Tag 062F (lemma-regular-koszul-regular, line 7265) and Lemma Tag 0CEM (lemma-koszul-regular-H1-regular, line 7301), turning the hypothesis of the item into the hypothesis of Lemma Tag 0665

proof.text: *The two Koszul complexes in degrees $\le2$ and reduction modulo $I$.* By [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex], $K_0(A,g_\bullet)=A$, $K_1(A,g_\bullet)=A^{\oplus m}$ with basis $e_1,\dots,e_m$ and $d_1(e_i)=g_i$, so $d_1(\sum_ia_ie_i)=\sum_ia_ig_i$; $K_2(A,g_\bullet)$ is free on $e_i\wedge e_j$ ($i<j$) with $d_2(e_i\wedge e_j)=g_ie_j-g_je_i$, so $d_1d_2=0$. The same holds over $\bar A$ with $\bar g_i$. Reducing coordinates modulo $I$ in these bases gives surjections $\pi_n:K_n(A,g_\bullet)\to K_n(\bar A,\bar g_\bullet)$ for $n=0,1,2$ with $\pi_{n-1}d_n=\bar d_n\pi_n$ (the matrices of $\bar d_n$ are those of $d_n$ reduced mod $I$), and $\ker\pi_1=I^{\oplus m}=\{\sum_ic_ie_i: c_i\in I\}$. This is the low-degree part of the source's exact sequence of complexes $0\to I\otimes_AK_\bullet(A,g_\bullet)\to K_\bullet(A,g_\bullet)\to K_\bullet(A/I,g_\bullet)\to0$ (exact because each $K_n(A,g_\bullet)$ is free).

source.place: Lemma Tag 0665 (lemma-H1-regular-in-quotient, line 7472), proof, first display (the exact sequence of complexes), with Definitions 0622/0623 (lines 6566-6600)

proof.text: *$I\cap K\subseteq IK$ (the source's injectivity of $\operatorname{Coker}(I^{\oplus m}\to I)\to\operatorname{Coker}(A^{\oplus m}\to A)$, written out).* Let $x\in I\cap K$. As $K=(g_1,\dots,g_m)$, write $x=\sum_ia_ig_i$ with $a_i\in A$ and put $a=\sum_ia_ie_i\in K_1(A,g_\bullet)$, so $d_1(a)=x$. By step 2, $\bar d_1(\pi_1(a))=\pi_0(d_1a)=\bar x=0$ since $x\in I$; so $\pi_1(a)$ is a $1$-cycle of $K_\bullet(\bar A,\bar g_\bullet)$, and by step 1 ($H_1=0$) there is $\beta\in K_2(\bar A,\bar g_\bullet)$ with $\bar d_2(\beta)=\pi_1(a)$. Choose $b\in K_2(A,g_\bullet)$ with $\pi_2(b)=\beta$ (lift each coordinate). Put $c=a-d_2(b)=\sum_ic_ie_i$. Then $\pi_1(c)=\pi_1(a)-\bar d_2(\pi_2b)=0$, so every $c_i\in I$ (step 2), and $\sum_ic_ig_i=d_1(c)=d_1(a)-d_1d_2(b)=x$. Hence $x=\sum_ic_ig_i\in IK$.

proof.text: *Conclusion.* Conversely $IK\subseteq I$ and $IK\subseteq K$ because both are ideals, so $IK\subseteq I\cap K$; with step 3, $I\cap K=IK$. (For $m=0$ both sides are $0$.)
